568.title: Salvation came to this house (Luke 19:1–10)
568.hook: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times over
568.howItsDone: Christians often read Zacchaeus when talking about repentance that changes behavior; in many churches, especially Catholic and Orthodox, making restitution is part of turning back after a wrong, and the story is read at the dedication of churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man shouted louder, and Jesus stood still and asked, what do you want? Who did you stop for? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Still in Jericho. You probably know the first half of this story: a short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see over the crowd, and Jesus stops underneath and calls him by name. "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Today we follow them inside. Because what Zacchaeus says at his own table, with the whole town grumbling outside, is one of the most surprising speeches in the Gospels. Nobody asks him for it. Jesus doesn't preach. Zacchaeus just stands up.
screen: `TODAY I MUST ABIDE AT THY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First the grumbling. Luke says they all murmured, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Tax collectors worked for Rome and often took more than they were owed, and a chief tax collector got rich on it. Then Zacchaeus stands and says, in the King James Bible: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Half to the poor. And fourfold back to anyone he cheated. Here's why fourfold is striking. The law of Moses had rules for paying back what you'd taken. For many wrongs, you returned it and added a fifth. But for a stolen sheep, Exodus says: "he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Zacchaeus reaches for the steepest standard, as if he'd stolen sheep from every one of them. And nobody told him to. Jesus never mentioned money. Being welcomed did what lectures hadn't. A few scholars point out that the Greek verbs are present tense, I give, I restore, and wonder if he's describing what he already does. Most read it as a new promise, there and then. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." This day. Today is one of Luke's favorite words. The angels used it at his birth: born this day. Jesus used it in Nazareth: this day, this scripture is fulfilled. And on the cross, he'll say today again. Salvation in Luke isn't only someday. It walks into a house, sits down to dinner, and changes how the money moves.
screen: then, large: `THIS DAY IS SALVATION COME TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repay someone generously. Settle and breathe. Think back. Is there anyone you owe something to? Money you borrowed and forgot, a favor never returned, credit you took that was really theirs, time you took from someone without giving back. Don't spiral into guilt. Just pick one. Now imagine paying it back, not exactly, but generously, more than you owe, the way Zacchaeus did. What would that look like? A check, a thank-you, a public word giving them the credit. If you pray, you can give thanks for being welcomed first. The bell holds the time.
Salvation came to this house. Welcomed before he changed, Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays fourfold, and Jesus says: this day, salvation.
screen: `SALVATION CAME TO THIS HOUSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today, salvation. Today, pay back the one thing you thought of, and add a little extra. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short man climbs a tree.
what it means: welcomed before he changed, Zacchaeus changes how his money moves, and salvation arrives today, in his house.
what a scholar hears: fourfold is the Exodus penalty for a stolen sheep, the present-tense verbs are debated, and today threads through Luke from the birth to the cross.

569.title: Ten pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
569.hook: Luke's version of the talents: be faithful with a little
569.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of gifts and talents as things given by God to be used for others, and churches often encourage people to discover and use their gifts in service, in the congregation and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salvation came to this house, and Zacchaeus paid back fourfold. Your line was today, salvation. What did you repay? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

Jericho is about a day's climb from Jerusalem. The crowd can feel it. Luke tells us exactly what's in the air: "they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear." Any day now. Maybe tomorrow. Jesus is heading into the capital, a healer and teacher with a crowd behind him, and people are ready for a coronation. So he tells them a story about a coronation that takes a long time to arrive, and about what to do in the meantime, with very little in your hands.

A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and then return. Jesus' listeners may well have recognized that. When Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to have his rule confirmed, and a delegation went after him to protest. In the story, too, the citizens send word: "We will not have this man to reign over us." Before he leaves, he calls ten servants and gives each of them one pound. In Greek, a mina: roughly a hundred days' wages. Not nothing, but not a fortune. And here's the big difference from Matthew's parable of the talents. There, servants get different amounts. Here, everyone gets exactly the same. His instruction in the King James Bible is "Occupy till I come." Occupy means do business, put it to work. When he returns, the first servant says: "Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds." And the answer: "Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities." A very little. Ten cities. The reward is wildly out of proportion to the test. Another made five. Then one comes and says: "Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin." Wrapped in a cloth, safe and useless, because he was afraid. Christians read this parable in more than one way. Most hear the nobleman as Christ, gone away and coming back, asking what his people did with what they were given. Some modern readers notice how harsh the nobleman is and hear a warning about earthly kings instead. Either way, the servants' question is ours: what do you do with a very little, while you wait?
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN A VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invest one small gift. Settle and breathe. Think of one small thing you have that you've been keeping wrapped up. A skill you don't use much, a little spare time, a modest amount of money, a talent for listening, cooking, fixing things, making people laugh. Nothing grand, just one pound. Notice what's kept it in the napkin: fear of getting it wrong, a sense that it's too small to matter. Now picture putting it to work this week, for someone else. One concrete step. If you pray, you can offer it back to God. The bell holds the time.
Ten pounds. Ten servants each given the same single pound, told to put it to work until their master returns, and rewarded for being faithful in a very little.
Your line: faithful in a very little. Today, take your one small gift out of the napkin and use it once. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

wrap it in a napkin and keep it safe.

fork.reveal: one servant says: "here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin" because he feared his master. safe, and unused.

original.note: Greek: a mina, a sum of money worth about a hundred days' wages. the King James Bible says pound.

trapdoor: what you thought: the same story as the talents.
what it means: everyone gets the same small gift, and the question is what you do with a very little while you wait.
what a scholar hears: the nobleman's journey echoes Archelaus going to Rome to claim his throne, and readers differ on whether the harsh nobleman stands for Christ or a warning about earthly kings.

570.title: The stones would shout (Luke 19:28–40)
570.hook: if these were silent, the stones would cry out
570.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, many churches hold a procession with palm branches, drawing on John's Gospel, and in years when Luke is read, the reading tells of cloaks on the road and the stones that would cry out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten pounds, one each, and a servant who kept his wrapped in a napkin. Your line was faithful in a very little. What small gift did you use? Day five hundred seventy.

Palm Sunday. Most people picture the same scene: crowds waving palm branches, children shouting hosanna. Now open Luke. He doesn't mention palms. Or hosanna. John's Gospel has the palms; Matthew and Mark have branches and hosannas. Luke's version is quieter in some ways, and louder in others. He tells it from just over the Mount of Olives, on the road down into Jerusalem, and he puts the noise somewhere unexpected. By the end of the scene, even the rocks on the roadside are in on it.

Jesus sends two disciples ahead to find a colt, in the King James Bible "whereon yet never man sat." They throw their cloaks on it, and as he rides, people spread their clothes on the road. Cloaks, not palms. It's what you did for a king: an old story in Kings has people spreading their garments under a new king's feet. And the prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humbly, riding on a colt. Then, as the road starts down the Mount of Olives and the whole city comes into view, "the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen." They sing: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest." Listen to that last part. It echoes the angels at his birth: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. The angels sang it to shepherds at the start. Now his followers sing it back as he comes to the city. Then some Pharisees in the crowd say: "Master, rebuke thy disciples." Maybe they're worried the Romans will hear the word king. And Jesus answers: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." It may echo Habakkuk, where "the stone shall cry out of the wall." There, the stones accuse injustice. Here, they'd praise. Some praise is too true to be silenced; if people won't say it, creation will.
screen: `A COLT, AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.`
then, large: `THE STONES WOULD IMMEDIATELY CRY OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise something aloud. Out loud, not just in your head. It may feel odd at first. Settle and breathe. Think of something good you've seen recently, a mighty work, as Luke says, large or small: a recovery, a kindness, a sunrise, a child's progress, a job well done. Now say it, actually say it, in a normal voice, even if you're alone. Thank you for this. This was good. If you pray, you can praise God aloud for it. If not, simply let your voice name the good thing. Then sit with the quiet that follows. The bell holds the time.
The stones would shout. As Jesus rides down toward Jerusalem, his followers praise God, and he says if they were silenced, the stones would cry out.
Your line: the stones would cry out. Today, say out loud to someone one good thing you've noticed about them. Don't leave it to the stones. Day five hundred seventy.

screen: `DAY 570 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HE WEPT OVER THE CITY.`

what a scholar hears: Luke has no palms or hosannas, his peace in heaven echoes the angels' song, and the shouting stones may echo Habakkuk 2:11.

571.title: He wept over the city (Luke 19:41–48)
571.hook: coming near Jerusalem, he weeps: if only you knew the things of peace
571.howItsDone: On the Mount of Olives, the small church of Dominus Flevit, Latin for the Lord wept, marks the traditional spot, and Christians around the world pray for the peace of Jerusalem and of cities in conflict, often using the words of Psalm 122.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cloaks on the road, a song of peace in heaven, and Jesus saying that if the crowd were silent, the stones would shout. Your line was the stones would cry out. What good thing did you say out loud? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Coming down the Mount of Olives today, the road bends, and suddenly the whole of Jerusalem is laid out across the valley: walls, domes, towers, the old city glowing gold in the late light. People stop and take photos. It's one of the great views on earth. Luke says that when Jesus came to that point, in the middle of the singing crowd, with the praise still ringing, he looked at the city. And he did something no one around him expected on a day of celebration.

In the King James Bible: "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it." The Greek word is not quiet tears. When Jesus stands at Lazarus's tomb in John's Gospel, the word is a gentler one, he shed tears. Here, Luke uses the word for weeping aloud, sobbing. In the middle of the parade. And then he speaks to the city as if it were a person he loves: "If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes." Jerusalem's name has long been heard as related to peace, shalom. The city of peace, and it doesn't know the things that make for peace. He goes on to describe enemies surrounding it, and walls thrown down, "because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." A visitation is God coming close. About forty years later, in the year 70, Roman armies besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the temple. Many Christians read these words as Jesus foreseeing that. But notice what he does with what he sees. He doesn't gloat or threaten. He weeps. It's grief, the way a parent grieves a child walking toward danger. The weeping and the action go together, too. He goes straight into the temple and drives out the sellers: "My house is the house of prayer." Then he teaches there daily. The leaders look for a way to destroy him, Luke says, but they can't, because "all the people were very attentive to hear him." Tears, then a cleansing, then teaching. Love for a city does all three.
screen: then, large: `IF THOU HADST KNOWN, EVEN THOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a city in conflict. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a city where there's fighting or deep division right now, near or far. It could be in the news, or it could be your own town, split down the middle. Picture it from a hillside, the way Jesus saw Jerusalem: the rooftops, the streets, the ordinary people inside. Let yourself feel something for them, even grief. If you pray, you can use the psalm's words: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee, and then, in your own words, ask for peace in the city you're picturing. If you don't, hold the city in your mind with care. The bell holds the time.
He wept over the city. Seeing Jerusalem in the middle of the celebration, Jesus sobs: if only you had known the things that belong to your peace.
screen: `HE WEPT OVER THE CITY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: if only you knew. Today, when you read news of a place at war, stop for one breath and let yourself care before you scroll on. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: The beloved son (Luke 20:1–19)
572.hook: the tenants kill the owner's son; the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone
572.howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the wicked tenants in Holy Week and often in late summer or autumn, and many churches use the cornerstone verse, from Psalm 118, in Easter worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he wept over the city. Your line was if only you knew. Which place, near or far, did you hold in mind for its peace? Day five hundred seventy-two.

It's the last week, and Jesus is teaching in the temple courts every day. The leaders come with a sharp question: by what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you the right? He answers with a question of his own, about John the Baptist, and they can't answer it without trouble either way. So nobody answers. And then he tells the crowd a story. A man plants a vineyard, rents it out to tenant farmers, and goes away for a long time. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants beat him and send him back with nothing. He sends a second. Same. A third. They wound him and throw him out. Today is what the owner does next.

In the King James Bible, the owner thinks out loud: "What shall I do? I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." Stop on that. Three servants beaten, and his answer is to send the person he loves most. It's not a clever plan. It's a hopeful one, maybe a foolish one. And the tenants see the son coming and reason the other way: this is the heir, kill him, and the vineyard is ours. They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Listeners in that crowd would have known the picture. In Isaiah, Israel is God's vineyard, planted with care. And the word beloved has been heard before in Luke. At the river, a voice from heaven called Jesus "my beloved Son." So Christians have long heard the story pointing at the one telling it. Luke says plainly who heard it as aimed at them: the chief priests and the scribes, who wanted to arrest him that hour and held back because they feared the people. Not a whole nation. A small circle of leaders in one tense week. Christians have sometimes forgotten that and turned this parable against Jewish people, and many churches today say so with regret. Then Jesus looks at the crowd and quotes a psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner." The builders look over a stone and toss it aside as useless. Later that very stone ends up holding the whole building together. The rejection is not the end of the story. It's the turn.
screen: `A STORY AIMED AT A FEW LEADERS.`
then, large: `THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the rejected stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you set aside as useless. A person you wrote off at work. An idea you dropped because someone laughed. A part of yourself you keep hidden, the clumsy part, the quiet part. Hold it in front of you for a moment, like a builder turning over a stone. What if this is the one that holds things together? Don't decide anything. Just look at it again, more slowly than you did the first time. If you pray, you can bring it to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
The beloved son. The owner's last and dearest messenger in the parable, the same words heaven spoke over Jesus at his baptism.
Your line: they will respect my son. Today, give one person you'd written off a second hearing, the way the owner kept on sending. Day five hundred seventy-two.

what it means: an owner who keeps sending, last of all his beloved son, and a rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone.
what a scholar hears: the vineyard echoes Isaiah 5, and 'beloved son' echoes the voice at the baptism; Luke names the chief priests and scribes as the ones who took it personally.

573.title: Children of the resurrection (Luke 20:20–40)
573.hook: trick questions about taxes and the dead: for all live to him
573.howItsDone: Christians often read Jesus's answer to the Sadducees at funerals and on All Souls' Day, and many pray for or remember their dead by name in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beloved son, sent last of all, and the stone the builders rejected. Your line was they will respect my son. Who got a second hearing from you? Day five hundred seventy-three.

A trick question is built so that every answer loses. Ask a politician whether they've stopped wasting money and watch them squirm. Luke says the leaders now send spies who pretend to be sincere, with a question like that. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Say yes, and the crowd hears a man who bows to Rome. Say no, and Rome hears a rebel. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose picture is on it. Caesar's. Then, in the King James Bible: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's." They go quiet. And then a second group arrives with a second trap, this one about the dead.

The second group are Sadducees, and Luke tells us they deny that there is any resurrection. So they spin a story to make the idea look ridiculous. Moses taught that if a man dies without children, his brother should marry the widow. Seven brothers, one after another, marry the same woman, and each one dies. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Jesus doesn't laugh at them. He says the life to come isn't a copy of this one. People there don't marry, because they can't die any more. They are, in the King James words, "the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." That phrase is a Hebrew way of speaking. A child of something is someone who belongs to it, whose life is shaped by it. Then Jesus goes back to Moses himself, to the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long after all three had died. Not the God they used to have. Their God, now. And then the line that is today's carry: "For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him." Here's a detail worth noticing. In this argument Jesus stands on the same side as the Pharisees, who also taught the resurrection. And Luke says some of the scribes answered, "Master, thou hast well said." After that, nobody dares ask him anything. Christians hear in all live to him a promise about the people they've lost: that they are not gone from God, even when they are gone from us.
screen: `THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, ISAAC AND JACOB.`
then, large: `FOR ALL LIVE UNTO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who died in hope. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've lost. A grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet if that's where your heart goes. Let their face come, or their voice, or their hands. You don't have to feel anything big. Just let them be near for a minute. If you pray, you can say their name to God and Jesus's words with it: all live unto him. If you don't, simply hold them with gratitude, and with whatever hope you have. The bell holds the time.
Children of the resurrection. Jesus's name for those who rise: people who belong to the life that doesn't die, and so belong to God.
Your line: all live to him. Today, say the name of someone you've lost out loud, to a friend or just to the room, and tell one small story about them. Day five hundred seventy-three.

what a scholar hears: 'children of the resurrection' is a Semitic idiom of belonging, and on this point Jesus sides with the Pharisees against the Sadducees.

574.title: More than all (Luke 20:41–21:4)
574.hook: beware showy religion; the widow gave out of her poverty
574.howItsDone: Christians often call small, costly gifts the widow's mite, and many churches read this story when inviting people to give, to charity or to the church, quietly and in proportion to what they have.

segments.voice: Yesterday, children of the resurrection, and a God of the living. Your line was all live to him. Whose name did you say out loud? Day five hundred seventy-four.

Picture the donation wall in a hospital lobby. Big brass plaques for the biggest gifts, smaller ones below, a long list of names in tiny print at the bottom. Now picture the temple courts in Jerusalem, where people drop their offerings into the collection chests. The wealthy come by, and their gifts are large, and people notice. Jesus is sitting where he can watch. He's just finished warning the crowd about religion that wants to be seen. And then a poor widow walks up and drops in two coins, the smallest coins there were. On a plaque, her name wouldn't make the list. Jesus turns to his friends and says something that rearranges the whole wall.

First the warning, in the King James words: "Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts." He's not attacking scribes as a group. Yesterday some of them told him he'd spoken well. He's describing a kind of faith that wants an audience, and he adds a harder line: they "devour widows' houses, and for a shew make long prayers." Then, straight after, a widow. Her two coins were lepta, from a Greek word meaning small, or thin. Luke has Jesus say: "Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had." More than all of them. Not more than each one. More than all of them put together. The gift is measured by what's left over afterward, and she has nothing left. Christians read this in two ways, and both are in the text. Most hear it as praise: total trust, giving from what you'd rather keep. Some scholars notice where Luke put it, right after the warning about leaders who swallow up widows' houses, and hear a lament too: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. Both readings agree on one thing. Jesus saw her when nobody else did.
